newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala peace talks resume Thursday in Mexico.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala peace talks resume Thursday in Mexico.

text.p: Guatemalan government peace negotiators will travel to Mexico City on Thursday to discuss the future of guerrilla fighters in a new round of peace talks with leftist rebels, a government official said.
Defence Minister General Julio Balconi told reporters on Wednesday the talks would centre on the political future of the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG in Spanish).

The URNG is an umbrella group of four guerrilla fronts, formed in 1982, one of the most violent periods during Guatemala's 36-year civil war which has left an estimated 100,000 dead and an additional 40,000 missing.

The United Nations has moderated sporadic Guatemalan peace negotiations since 1991, but talks picked up earlier this year with a ceasefire and the signing of an important land and labour accord. Both sides hope to sign a final treaty by the year's end.
Two weeks ago rebels and the government signed a landmark agreement in Mexico City, reducing Guatemala's powerful army by one-third and limiting its post-war role.
Now the focus is on the guerrillas' future. URNG membership is against the law in Guatemala. An estimated 1,000 fighters and commanders live in hiding or in exile.
It is widely believed the URNG wants to form a legitimate political party with representation in Congress.
Chief government peace negotiator Gustavo Porras recently told reporters this would require changes to the law.
Porras said the touchy subject of war crimes and human rights abuses by both the army and guerrillas would also come up in this round of talks.

"Because of opposition to a general amnesty we will seek a legal framework to establish which acts will be included (in an amnesty) so that matters outside of the armed conflict aren't protected," said Porras.

Porras said the killing of a guerrilla leader in combat, for example, would fall under the amnesty. But amnesty would not cover army personnel linked to assassinations of judges, political figures, and academics off the battlefield.
